content: 1. Once the calendar is finalized, preparations for fieldwork can commence, and recruitment and enrollment in the field can begin. 2. Time-location sampling involves multiple stages, and the process for selecting sampling units at each stage must be clearly defined. This includes documenting the sampling frames, cluster sizes, the number of individuals sampled in each cluster, and reasons for nonresponse. 3. A protocol checklist and the time-location sampling (TLS) section of the survey design checklist can assist in planning and development of standard operating procedures (SOPs). 4. By the end of the formative assessment, investigators should have a comprehensive understanding of the types of locations or venues where the target population can be accessed. This assessment may uncover unexpected venues or locations. 5. It is essential to ensure that all types of locations or venues are represented in the venue sampling frame to avoid bias. 6. Recruitment strategies should be flexible to accommodate the unstructured nature of public locations or venues. This allows the field team to systematically and efficiently recruit participants without rigid procedures that may not fit all situations. 7. Geographical boundaries for each location or venue should be clearly defined and agreed upon by the team during mapping. 8. A standardized introduction script for recruiters and the survey should be developed and rehearsed for each sampling event. 9. Recruitment should be conducted in small teams of at least two people to ensure safety and adherence to SOPs. 10. All information relevant to each sampling stage should be documented and retained, including time-location units, procedures for selecting sampling units, cluster sizes, and nonresponse data. 11. Nonresponse reasons may include refusal by venue managers to allow sampling events or individual respondents declining consent or failing to complete data collection stages. 12. Clear SOPs should be created to compile an exhaustive list of locations and venues where individuals can be accessed for interviews. This ensures a comprehensive sampling frame that includes all relevant time-location clusters. 13. Venue information can be sourced from key informant interviews, focus group discussions, websites, newspapers, and field observations. 14. A location or venue data-collection form should be used to record all relevant information about each venue, including its suitability for the survey, the presence of the target population, and logistical considerations. 15. The formative assessment may reveal locations or venues where the target population gathers but where it is unsafe or impossible to approach, recruit, or interview them. Investigators should evaluate the potential sampling bias introduced by excluding these locations. 16. Criteria for venue suitability should be established to determine whether a location or venue can be included in the sampling frame. 17. Attendance patterns at venues should be analyzed to identify variations in attendance by time of day or day of the week. If significant differences exist, the same venue may need to be included in the sampling frame multiple times to account for these variations. 18. Multiplicity refers to the possibility that individuals may attend multiple venues during the sampling period, increasing their probability of being sampled. This can be addressed by asking participants how often they attend other venues and using this information to calculate individual-level weights. 19. Approach criteria should be used by survey staff to decide who should be approached for recruitment into the survey. These criteria should be consistent across all recruiters to avoid bias. 20. Community liaisons, who are members of the surveyed community, can help identify potential participants and establish rapport with the community. 21. Sampling events typically last between 2 and 4 hours. The duration may vary to allow for more recruitment at low-volume clusters or less recruitment at high-volume clusters. 22. For venues active for extended periods, such as 6 PM to 2 AM, the time can be divided into separate periods to avoid excessive time spent at a single venue. 23. Venue owners or managers may need to be approached for permission to conduct sampling events. If permission is denied, information about the venue should still be collected to assess potential sampling bias. 24. In cases where it is not possible to conduct interviews or testing at the selected venue, alternative arrangements should be made, such as using a nearby tent or van or scheduling interviews for another day. 25. Steps to determine the venue universe include developing an SOP for creating the sampling frame, identifying and describing locations or venues, observing the venues, and reviewing and finalizing the venue universe description. 26. Data elements required for each venue include the number of attendees, time slots, attendance patterns, multiplicity, safety, and logistics. 27. Observers should establish rapport with venue owners or managers, talk to venue staff and attendees, and use venue suitability criteria to determine whether the venue is appropriate for sampling. 28. The venue universe information should be reviewed for completeness and accuracy, and suitable venues and time periods should be included in the time-location cluster sampling frame. 29. Venue observation forms should document venue type, name, code, contact information, address, attendance patterns, logistical considerations, and any barriers to recruitment. 30. Observations should include demographic characteristics, seasonal variations, mobility patterns, and safety concerns. Detailed sketches of venue layouts and boundaries should also be included. 31. If interviews or testing cannot be conducted at the venue, alternative locations or other-day appointments should be considered, with appropriate measures to minimize nonresponse and maintain confidentiality.
